## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Byagghajātaka* (Ja 272), translated in modern listings as *The Tiger*, is a canonical birth story belonging to the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. The narrative opening relates that the Buddha delivered the story while residing at Jetavana in reference to Kokālika, following an incident in which the senior disciples Sāriputta and Moggallāna refused Kokālika's invitation to accompany him to his home region [SuttaCentral].

In the core tale, tree spirits living in a forest become repulsed by the stench of rotting carcasses left behind by a resident lion and tiger and scheme to frighten the two predators away [Hart 2017]. Once the dangerous felines abandon the area, local villagers lose their fear of the forest, chop down the trees for agricultural land, and inadvertently evict the foolish tree spirits from their habitat [Hart 2017]. Modern environmental scholarship notes the narrative as an early Buddhist reflection on ecological interdependence and landscape change driven by human encroachment [Hart 2017].

No cross-language parallels are recorded on SuttaCentral or detected by DharmaNexus [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Text-reuse analysis conducted by DharmaNexus records three matching segments shared internally with the commentary, the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), covering the canonical text (§0.4–2.4) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral catalogs four modern translations of the text across four languages [SuttaCentral].
